Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. The backpack slides go quickly and prime the room; the turn-and-talks come after them. Keep it about the roads, not the people: nothing in the backpack is about effort or character. Nobody has to share what’s in their own backpack. Keep each turn-and-talk open: for you, or for people you know. Test the Crenshaw clip on the school network before the talk.

Every student in the room

Challenges stack up for many students, and for students of color and other minority groups more of them often land in the same backpack. Money, being the only one, adult jobs at home, long commutes and health that gets squeezed are often invisible at an independent school; name them plainly and move on so nobody feels spotted.

Slides and notes

Tap any slide to present from there.

Slide 1 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Open warm: “Today is about why this toolkit exists. Short version: your life doesn’t come in separate pieces.”

Slide 2 · Notes

BEFORE THE TALK: test that this clip plays on the school network and the room’s screen. 2 MINUTES. Play the whole clip, then click to her intersection picture. Link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qTweF3o5ZyU

Slide 3 · Notes

2 MINUTES. Crenshaw coined the word in 1989 to show how Black women could fall through the cracks of laws that looked at race or gender one at a time. Next slide: everyone has their own crossing.

Slide 4 · Notes

2 MINUTES. Keep it about lanes, not people: the hurdles come with the lane. Say: “Same race, same finish. Not the same track.”

Slide 5 · Notes

About 45 seconds a slide. Say: “Watch the backpack. Nothing here is about effort or character.” When someone seems checked out, sometimes they’re just out of hours.

Slide 6 · Notes

45 SECONDS. Lots of students carry adult jobs at home. It can be a source of pride and a real load on the same day.

Slide 7 · Notes

45 SECONDS. Say it plainly and move on; nobody should feel spotted. Money is often invisible at a school like ours, and students cover for it.

Slide 8 · Notes

45 SECONDS. Sleep is one health example of many. Ask: “What else gets squeezed when the day is full before it starts?”

Slide 9 · Notes

45 SECONDS. Being the only one takes energy most people never notice spending. Don’t point at anyone.

Slide 10 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Say: “These pieces come with the road a student is on, and for many students of color and other minority groups, more of them land in the same backpack. A wellness program has to be built with that in mind. That’s what Crenshaw means.”

Slide 11 · Notes

3 MINUTES. Turn and talk. The backpack primed them; now let them add what it missed. Share for you or for people you know.

Slide 12 · Notes

3 MINUTES. Take a few answers and name them back. Nobody speaks for a group.

Slide 13 · Notes

1 MINUTE. This is the heart of Crenshaw’s point for a school: advice built for one kind of student misses the student where several roads meet.

Slide 14 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Struggle is real, and so is what students draw on. Point to the hands: “Nobody here should carry the whole thing alone.” Next: turn and talk.

Slide 15 · Notes

3 MINUTES. Turn and talk with the people next to you. Next slide: share out.

Slide 16 · Notes

3 MINUTES. Take a few answers and name them back. Nobody speaks for a group.

Slide 17 · Notes

2 MINUTES. This is the why behind the toolkit. The department’s priority is the mental health and wellness of the whole school community, and intersections shape that health. So every lesson is built with students at the intersections in mind from the start.

Slide 18 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Let the line sit. This is the whole reason the toolkit exists.

Slide 19 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Name the real people: “Ms. Garcia, Dr. Wilson, your advisor. Our doors are open.”

Slide 20 · Notes

1 MINUTE. Close warm. Point out where to find the toolkit and that every page lists a person first.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students hear Kimberlé Crenshaw explain intersectionality in her own words and see how challenges can stack up: less time, being the go-between, money, health and being the only one land in the same backpack and set a different starting line, every week. They name what else stacks up, then name the sources of strength their identities also hold. They leave knowing the toolkit is built for every starting line, and that nobody has to carry it alone.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • Kimberlé Crenshaw’s 2-minute clip “What is Intersectionality?” (NAIS). It plays inside the web deck when you click the Watch slide; the PowerPoint slide opens it on YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qTweF3o5ZyU . Test it on the school network and the room’s screen before the talk.
  • The Student Toolkit link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 5 minCrenshaw’s clip and her traffic intersection
  2. 7 minNot everyone starts from the same line; the backpack fills one piece at a time; it stacks
  3. 8 minTurn and talk: what else can stack up for students here? Share out; one-size advice misses people
  4. 8 minYour identity also holds sources of strength. Turn and talk, then share out
  5. 5 minA toolkit for every starting line, mental health is where it all meets, don’t carry it alone, close

Short on time (15 minutes)

The Crenshaw clip and intersection, the starting line, the five backpack slides and “It stacks,” one turn and talk with its share-out, the strength slide, then don’t carry it alone and the closing slide.

Before you teach
Nobody speaks for a group.

Invite answers about “you, or people you know.” Never ask a student to explain their culture, faith or family to the room.

The weight is in the roads, not the student.

The backpack has no wearer on purpose. Talk about what comes with a road, never about who a student is.

Strength is real too.

After the stack, name the sources of strength identity holds and let students add their own.

Money is real here.

Say it plainly once and keep going. The “I’m good, I already ate” slide works because it doesn’t point at anyone.

If something heavy comes up.

Thank the student, keep it short in the room, and connect them with a counselor that day.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Challenges stack.

For many students of color and other minority groups, several pieces land at once. A wellness program has to be built with that in mind.

Families draw on different things.

Faith, culture, a language, elders, a team. Treat each as a real strength, never as a curiosity.

Money shapes friendships.

Trips, dinners out and the right shoes cost money. Students with less often do quiet math nobody sees.

One-size advice misses people.

“Just get more sleep” misses the student who gets home at 7 and fills out forms for family at 10. Start with where a student actually is.

What the research says

The term intersectionality comes from legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw, who used it to describe how race and sex together shaped Black women’s experiences in ways neither one alone explains.

Crenshaw, 1989, University of Chicago Legal Forum

Teens aged 13 to 18 need 8 to 10 hours of sleep a night for health, learning, mood and attention.

American Academy of Sleep Medicine consensus statement (Paruthi et al., 2016, Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine)

Across many studies, a positive sense of ethnic-racial identity is linked to better well-being and fewer depressive symptoms in young people.

Rivas-Drake et al., 2014, Child Development

Teens who felt connected at school had lower risks of emotional distress, suicidal thoughts and substance use as adults.

Steiner et al., 2019, JAMA Pediatrics
